title: Bosses embrace AI, but count the tech’s cost
full_text:
Australian bosses are rolling out AI with their “eyes wide open”, with the technology still promising productivity gains despite surging costs.
While there’s a big appetite among corporate Australia to embrace the technology, less talked about is the high entry price to join the AI race. This is the so-called “tokenomics” behind the growing cost of using massive processing power for AI models.
Investors want to hear how companies are using the tech, but there is an emerging view that AI spending can’t be at any cost. Boards are now demanding greater accountability around returns from specific projects, given the scale of both upfront and ongoing investment.
Global tech consultant Gartner last month forecast that global spending by corporates on software – which takes in AI – will jump as much as 15.5 per cent this year, on top of 14 per cent growth last year. Its these kinds of projections that are spurring on the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent by hyperscalers building data centres.
Several companies in recent weeks have called out additional costs from their tech spending, but have framed this as productivity investment. Locally, costs are spread between capex, representing new investment and opex, representing ongoing expenses of maintaining tech.
Commonwealth Bank, for one, saw its operating expenses jump 5.6 per cent over the past year – well ahead of inflation – partly due to tech investment driving additional costs. Suncorp also flagged higher tech spending, although this was mostly offset by savings elsewhere in the business.
Banks and software companies are clearly more exposed to surging tech expense charges, given they remain heavy users. Some companies are now talking about opening around guardrails to ensure that embracing massive processing power doesn’t come with unchecked bills.
“Cloud [storage] is an interesting concept because back in the day, if you had a data storage challenge, you’d have to put a business case together to go and buy some hardware. Now it’s sort of almost like all-you-can-eat,” Suncorp chief executive Steve Johnston tells The Australian.
But he warns costs can become invisible until it’s too late – “until they appear in your P&L. There’s a need now to create discipline inside the organisation,” he says.
Telstra, another big adopter of the technology, says you need to be thinking about the cost side from the very beginning. The telco has a control plane in place to monitor real-time costs, performance and safety across hundreds of AI-powered projects.
Telstra’s Vicki Brady says AI is “absolutely fundamental and an enabler of our business”, but her executives were acutely aware of the cost implications early on. This involved putting in place a framework to use AI and allowing it to scale it across thousands of employees without letting costs outweigh benefits.
“We’re actually seeing that we’re able to drive our usage of AI up, while not growing costs. So net, we’re absolutely seeing benefits from AI,” Brady says.
Her comments come as a Treasury advisory paper this week argued Australia needs to harness AI to help lift sagging productivity back to a long-run baseline of 1.2 per cent over the next five years – though there’s a risk it could fall short depending on adoption rates.
CBA’s Matt Comyn confirmed costs are running higher than expected at his bank, but are being managed within a fixed investment budget. At the same time, CBA has put a number on what it calls gross AI productivity benefits, which are forecast to double over the coming year to $400m. This means after years in the rollout, benefits will exceed investment costs for the first time.
“We believe we can get substantially more done in 2027,” Comyn says of the productivity gains. The lift in productivity offers more scope for flexibility in managing costs.
National Australia Bank’s Andrew Irvine also makes a strong case for AI inside his bank, where 2500 software developers are now using GenAI-enhanced coding tools. But cost monitoring, he says, is non-negotiable.
“All of our business cases would be very strongly linked to cost-benefit scenarios,” Irvine tells The Australian.
“They haven’t accelerated at a level that would make me uncomfortable at this stage.” Some executives are thinking about more proactive ways to manage AI costs. Many process-driven tasks don’t require cutting-edge – and costly – frontier models; a more extreme step is capping monthly usage among the highest-use employees.
But all are watching the bigger picture. Wesfarmers’ Rob Scott says that, like any investment, you have to go in aware of the risks.
“You’ve absolutely got to go in with your eyes wide open,” Scott says. “You’ve got to have a really good understanding of what the cost is, from both a people and a token cost, with your initiatives.” Still, across a business that spans Bunnings, Kmart and Officeworks, Scott points to some strong operational and commercial outcomes from Wesfarmers’ “people-first, digitally enabled” rollout. This includes Google Cloud’s agentic AI shopping assistant, now used across its retail brands such as Kmart and Target by more than a million customers.
Scott argues it has so far driven a doubling of online conversion rates and larger checkout baskets.
On the back end, Bunnings has saved half a million employee hours on administrative tasks, freeing up more time for frontline staff.
Software vendors, meanwhile, are becoming more sensitive to customer pushback over surging costs and are introducing more economical models. Alphabet chief executive Sundar Pichai recently unveiled a new suite of Google’s Gemini AI tools that he says “hits the sweet spot of performance and cost”.
Industrial companies with heavy fixed-cost investments hold AI to a higher hurdle. BlueScope Steel’s Tania Archibald says there’s promise in AI boosting workforce productivity, but the gains need to be tangible. “What I struggle with is how you actually see that impact in the bottom line,” Archibald says. “We’ve just got to be very cautious about what investments we’re making, and how we actually hold ourselves to account on the benefits that are actually being delivered.” Qantas chief executive Vanessa Hudson says AI spending should be approached like any capex program – which is focused on unlocking productivity and efficiency to deliver better outcomes for customers, while also delivering for the business and shareholders. johnstone@theaustralian.com.au
